Source [S2], specifically Equation (11), defines the blur loss exactly as $L_{blur} =  rac{1}{m}  sum_{x  in X}  | |  hat{B}(x) - B(x) | |_2^2$. The notation matches perfectly: $m$ is the number of pixels, $X$ is the set of pixels, $ hat{B}(x)$ is the simulated blurry image, and $B(x)$ is the input blurry image. The summation is over all pixels $x  in X$, and the term inside the summation is the squared L2 norm (Euclidean distance) between the predicted and actual blurry images. Therefore, every fact in the claim is present and supported by the evidence.

Event loss is $\mathcal{L}_{event} = \frac{1}{m(p-1)} \sum_{i=1}^{p-1} \sum_{x \in X} \| \hat{E}(x, t_i, t_{i+1}) - E(x, t_i, t_{i+1}) \|_2^2$ [S2].

The claim provides the mathematical formula for the event loss $L_{event}$ as $L_{event} =  rac{1}{m(p-1)}  sum_{i=1}^{p-1}  sum_{x  in X}  | |  hat{E}(x, t_i, t_{i+1}) - E(x, t_i, t_{i+1}) | | _2^2$. Source [S2] explicitly defines this loss in Equation (8) (and the text below it) as minimizing the differences between predicted and actual events on all $m$ pixels $x  in X$ among all input views, summed over $p-1$ intervals. The formula in the claim matches the structure and components described in the evidence: the summation over pixels $x$ and time intervals $i=1$ to $p-1$, the squared L2 norm difference between simulated events $ hat{E}$ and real events $E$, and the normalization factor $ rac{1}{m(p-1)}$.
